Thanks for adding these. Two things on `cf33b01a9`:

The four delete tests check `table.newScan().planFiles()` with `doesNotThrowAnyException()`, but `planFiles()` is lazy. `ManifestGroup.plan()` builds the `DeleteFileIndex` right away, but data manifests are only read when the iterable is consumed, so the step that matches deletes to data files by partition value never runs. body:
Getting a bit long, hard to read...
Shall we refactor the documentation a bit

```suggestion
- The index is **reused across triggers and restored on failover** while it matches the head of the target branch: the head is the snapshot the index was built from, or the converter's own commit for the last planned staging snapshot directly on top of it. Each cycle applies its staging snapshot's changes to the index, so consecutive conversions do not rebuild it.
- Otherwise the next trigger **rebuilds the index** from the target branch head, reading the equality columns of every live data file. This happens:
    - on cold start without a checkpoint, and on the first trigger after restoring state written by an older Iceberg version
    - after any other commit on the target branch, e.g. compaction, external writes, rollback, or replace-main (see *Concurrent commits on the target branch* below)
    - after restoring a checkpoint that predates the latest conversion commit
    - when the last planned conversion did not commit
    - when an earlier rebuild did not finish
```
title: Review comment on apache/iceberg#18674 (docs/docs/flink-maintenance.md)

body:
Might just remove the first sentence after the changes above.

```suggestion
- On restart, the planner rediscovers its position by walking the target branch for the marker property `equality-convert-staging-snapshot` written by the committer. If that marker is no longer reachable on the target branch (target was rolled back, replace-main'ed, or the marker snapshot was expired) the planner fails and requires manual intervention.
```

@huaxingao Thanks, you're right. I tried the example on the 4.2 tests (MoR UPDATE, with the concurrent change committed right before the UPDATE commits, same setup as the tests in this PR). With the current check the UPDATE fails; with this PR it commits.

Without a subquery on the same table, the UPDATE's result depends only on rows that match its condition. All of those are in data files it modifies, so the narrowed check still catches every concurrent delete that changes the result. Concurrent inserts are still checked by `validateNoConflictingDataFiles()` under SERIALIZABLE. The difference is only for UPDATEs whose subquery reads other rows of the same table, and the write can't tell those apart: it only gets the command and the target scan's filter.

body:
The `1.10.x` branch currently uses Guava `33.4.8-jre`, which is within the affected version range for CVE-2026-102554 (versions earlier than `33.7.2`).

This vulnerability affects Java deserialization of certain Guava collection implementations, potentially leading to excessive memory allocation and denial of service.

Since Iceberg bundles and relocates Guava, users consuming the `1.10.x` release line would continue to receive the affected Guava version unless we upgrade it.

The purpose of this PR is to backport the Guava security fix to the `1.10.x` maintenance branch, allowing users to receive the updated dependency without having to move to a newer Iceberg minor version.

Additionally, this change replaces the affected Guava `Queues` usages with equivalent JDK collection implementations to ensure compatibility with Shadow JAR minimization.

body:
@pvary
> What are the expectation of the time for the commits?

Well below the commit interval. Our target is about 3 minutes from a change to its visibility. With a commit interval of 60 to 90 s, the conversion should take at most about 80 s, or about 40 s so that one retry still fits.

> Is a worst case full read acceptable?

Not on large tables, I think. When the changes are spread over the key space, every commit reads the key column of the whole table. Our two largest CDC tables are unpartitioned, with about 150 to 160 data files and 1.7 and 2.4 billion rows. Amoro already reads all of these files after each commit to turn the equality deletes into position deletes. It runs one task per data file in parallel, and still takes 14 s and 43 s. I haven't measured the conversion on our storage yet, but doing that in one coordinator on every commit is too expensive.

So I'd document in part 2 that the conversion suits tables where the key filter or the partition spec prunes most data files, such as increasing keys with changes on recent rows. Tables with changes spread over many rows need an index behind `KeyPositionResolver`, as a follow-up.

body:
The specification states that a write-default expression is evaluated for any record written after the field was added, provided the writer does not supply a value. This defines which records receive a default, but leaves the evaluation frequency of non-deterministic functions ambiguous: once per row, per write operation, or per file/commit.

For example, ANSI SQL (and Spark) evaluate current_timestamp() once per statement, so a batch "INSERT INTO t SELECT ..." writing 10M rows to a table with a created_at TIMESTAMP write-default of current_timestamp() would assign the same timestamp to every row. In contrast, a streaming sink might evaluate the expression per record or per checkpoint, producing different timestamps across rows. Furthermore, after checkpoint replay, re-emitted records could receive new values, making the write non-idempotent. Consequently, the same table metadata could produce different results across engines. To avoid this ambiguity, I suggest explicitly specifying that non-deterministic functions in write-default expressions must be evaluated at most once per write operation, consistent with SQL statement-level semantics. Alternatively, if per-record evaluation i […]

body:
```suggestion
Schemas are matched by column name. The table schemas are checked starting with the current schema, then from newest to oldest. A table schema which matches the record exactly is preferred over one which needs a conversion (for example `Integer` to `Long`), so a record which has the shape of an older table schema is written with that schema, even if it would also fit the current one. The exceptions are older table schemas which use a column name that belongs to a different column in the current schema, for example after a column was dropped and added again, or renamed and its name reused. Data written with such a schema is stored under column IDs which queries on the current schema do not read, so these schemas are only used when the record fits no other table schema, not even with a conversion. In that case the affected values are not visible through the current schema.
```

body: Right, released clients don't send it. Today the Java client only sets a User-Agent when `rest.client.user-agent` is configured, so servers see the Apache HttpClient default (they can still identify old Java clients from the `X-Client-Version` header). The spec can't change what's already shipped, which is why the advisory rules say servers SHOULD NOT reject a request whose header is absent, incomplete, or malformed. The MUST is for clients that follow this format from now on, so a server can always rely on the library token being there. With a SHOULD, it couldn't rely on it even for new clients. This is also the wording the vote passed on. The client changes that add the token (Java, Python, Go, Rust) are ready and will go out once this merges.

body: manuzhang asked which status code a refusing server should return (https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17727#discussion_r4290683598). 400 is the standard client-error response. The Java client raises it as a BadRequestException with the server's message and doesn't retry it, so naming the refused version tells the user what to upgrade. Other codes send the wrong signal: 403 reads as a permissions problem, and this header must not be used for authorization; 409 is a commit conflict, which the Java client retries. It's a SHOULD, so a server can still pick a different code.

Logical checks that operating data has not changed:
- Data files were added

- Data files are missing

Physical checks for reference integrity

body: I think that `timestamptz` makes more sense than `timestamp`. Timestamp with time zone represents a point in time that will be shown to users in the SQL session time zone. If we were to use timestamp without time zone, the only difference would be that the time would be shown to all users the same way. In either case, the value is stored as some offset from the unix epoch. I think showing the value in the session time zone is what users expect so we should use `timestamptz`.

body:
This is wider than `Evaluator`. `SparkV2Filters` notes that Iceberg expressions are 2-valued (it rewrites `NOT IN` to `notNull && notIn`), and `StrictEvalVisitor` also treats `notEq` / `notIn` as matching all-null files. Changing only `Evaluator` would make it disagree with the metrics evaluators.

Should expressions become 3-valued across the evaluators, or stay 2-valued and be documented? Happy to do either.

Did have a discussion on this with @pvary : It's not really sophisticated to have such a switch on the exact type of the `ScanTask` here. We believe that the `ScanTask` implementations themselves should be able to tell us, what are their referenced files if there are any. That would be the right level of abstraction.

As an implementation what we have in mind is to have some interface like `HasReferencedFiles` with a single function `referencedFiles()` returning a collection of `ContentFile`s.
Then here in the decryptor we can iterate the list of `ScanTasks` verify that they implement the new interface (throw if not) and ask them to give us their referenced files.

You are right, I was rushing things a bit here - the design doc was recommending this change, but now I think it shouldn't.

I'll amend the design doc and revert the changes here and make the bearer manager strictly opt-in. We'll keep inferring `oauth2` (v1) from `token`, as today.

Let's just keep in mind though that the new OAuth2 manager v2 (#18756) will _not_ handle `token`. To upgrade, users of `token` will have 2 options:

- Upgrade to `oauth2` v2 and provide valid OAuth2 credentials instead of a raw token.
- Upgrade to `bearer` and keep using raw tokens as before.

I'm considering closing this implementation in favor of documenting the limitation and a verified workaround (docs PR to follow). #18748 stays open. Here is a summary:

**Design.** When every partition spec is partitioned only by equality fields, the writer also emits each equality delete for every older spec it saw at startup, as long as the key column types match. An unpartitioned older spec gets a global delete. Checkpoint state keeps one delete manifest per spec (serializer v3), and a delete that cancels an insert from the same checkpoint stays a position delete. This fixes deletes against rows committed in earlier checkpoints for those tables, but every variant runs into a tension between covering older specs, read cost, and the spec lifecycle:

- **Read cost.** For unpartitioned → bucketed evolution, every upsert adds a global equality delete. That adds delete-processing work across all partitions, and as long as those deletes are emitted and live, they keep the old spec referenced. Skipping specs that no longer hold data needs a liveness check in the writer, which loads metadata in every subtask and races with concurrent commits.

There is no common parent of `DataFile`, `DeleteFile` and `ColumnFile` that we could use here, unfortunately. We have a couple of ways to solve this:
1) In the future if we introduce something like an `EncryptedFile` we could introduce a variation that returns the common interface, but for now we don't have anything like that. This might be a long-term solution.
2) We could adapt/wrap a `ColumnFile` to seem like a `ContentFile` and then we can return them as part of the list. Might seem a nasty workaround, I probably wouldn't be in favor of this option.
3) Technically, `ContentFile` contains the column files. In the decryptor we can get the `ColumnFile`s if a file is a `DataFile` instance.

I think I'd prefer 3) because then there is a single place where we change the code for column file coverage and we get it everywhere, where the decryptor is used.

About the other question: I have considered that option too. What I wanted to avoid is to have a default implementation that compiles and runs but then silently misses some files in case of an implementation that doesn't override it. > @MonkeyCanCode thanks for confirming that at least #18378 fixes the original issue. The reason you're seeing this particular stack trace is because we register the `FileIO` instance to be closed in `RESTSessionCatalog` but the `RESTSessionCatalog` itself is never closed, hence we're leaking `FileIO` instances there. We're still closing them but we're issuing a WARN msg to tell users that this is a resource leak. The same is true for the executor used in `RESTMetricsReporter` as its closing is tied to `RESTSessionCatalog` being closed.

Thanks @nastra, that makes sense. To clarify the direction for the remaining part:
1. Is closing the catalog the preferred fix (https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/59952) plus SparkCatalog/SparkSessionCatalog passing close() through (this PR)?
2. Separately, would you accept letting the metrics executor's idle thread exit (allowCoreThreadTimeOut, no inherited thread-locals)? I tested it on top of https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18378, and released Spark Connect sessions are no longer retained even without catalog close. The FileIO warning remains in that case, as expected.

Indeed we don't carry over any defaults from the catalog properties, so if the `SessionContext` does not contain a token endpoint, but contains other OAuth2 properties, the default catalog internal token endpoint would be used.

Why I think it's generally not a good idea to merge catalog properties with context properties: consider the following setup:

* Catalog properties:
  ```properties
  rest.auth.oauth2.issuer-url=issuer1
  rest.auth.oauth2.client-id=client1
  rest.auth.oauth2.client-secret=secret1
  rest.auth.oauth2.resource=resource1
  ```

* Context properties (note no client secret, maybe hinting at a public client):
  ```properties
  rest.auth.oauth2.issuer-url=issuer2
  rest.auth.oauth2.client-id=client2
  rest.auth.oauth2.audience=audience2
  ```

If we blindly merge the two, we'd get:

```properties
rest.auth.oauth2.token-endpoint=issuer2
rest.auth.oauth2.client-id=client2
rest.auth.oauth2.client-secret=secret1
rest.auth.oauth2.resource=resource1
rest.auth.oauth2.audience=audience2
```

Which is almost certainly a wrong setup.

I have asked an AI to collect the possible failure scenarios, and distributed them based on whether they can be reried-or-not.

Transient: retrying the same delta works
- Storage throttling or outages: S3/GCS/ADLS 503 or 429 errors last longer than the FileIO retries.
- Credential refresh hiccup: an STS/IMDS timeout, or the REST catalog's refresh endpoint is briefly down.
- Replication lag: a replica doesn't have a just-committed manifest list yet, so the read returns 404.
- Catalog outage: table.refresh() fails before the delta even starts.

Already ends in a rebuild
- Snapshot expiry by another engine: it deletes manifest lists mid-read, and on the next trigger the walk breaks and the planner rebuilds.

Never succeeds, though a rebuild at the head would (the delta is stuck)
- Leaked equality delete, later cleaned up: validateTargetDeleteFiles fails on every trigger.
- Lost metadata of an older snapshot: a lifecycle rule, cleanup script or orphan-file removal deleted a manifest list the head no longer uses.
- Corrupt manifest from a buggy writer: it was later replaced by a manifest merge or rewrite, but the delta still reads it.

Reproduced with DuckDB 2.0.0's Iceberg extension as the client, on `apache/iceberg-rest-fixture:latest` built from `b0df3ca`, using the JDBC catalog on SQLite.

Two `MERGE` statements committed through `/v1/transactions/commit`, with a proxy releasing both commit requests at the same moment. Both returned 204, and one write was lost in 12 of 12 rounds:
- guarded on empty `main`, same new row (4 of 4)
- guarded on an existing `main` snapshot, different new rows (4 of 4)
- guarded on an existing `main` snapshot, update to the same row (4 of 4)

So this also affects commits on a table with existing data, including appends of unrelated rows, and not only a guard on empty `main`. The catalog log showed the same sequence: `Cannot commit ... metadata location has changed`, `Retrying task after failure: sleepTimeMs=100`, `Nothing to commit.`

When the second commit was released after the first had finished, it got the expected 409.

For comparison, AWS S3 Tables with the same client lost no writes in 36 rounds of concurrent merges.

Suggested text changes -
**In Column Files**

A column file stores the fields listed in its `field_ids`. A listed struct includes all fields nested in it. In this section, a struct _contains_ a field if the field is nested in the struct at any depth.

Each ID in `field_ids` must identify a field in the schema of the file it modifies, or a row lineage field required by [Writing Column Files](#writing-column-files). The schema of a data file is the table schema. The schema of a leaf manifest is the tracked file schema. Fields nested in a list or map must not be listed in `field_ids`.

If a column file of an entry lists a struct, no other column file of that entry can list a field that the struct contains.

**In Writing Column Files**

The added column files must list each field that the update changes, or a struct that contains that field. If an update changes whether a struct is null, the update changes that struct.

+1, I think these rules are right and we need them. The current text has two problems with structs:

1. Reading: L1811 says a listed struct includes its nested fields, but L1840 only reads a field from a column file if its own ID is listed. So with `field_ids: [2]`, `customer.name` (3) would be read from the data file.

2. Writing: if column file A lists `[3]` and a later update adds column file B with `[2]`, L1833 only removes ID 2, so A keeps `[3]`. The reader then reads the old `name` from A. Your change to also remove the fields a listed struct contains fixes this.

One small suggestion: could we put "no other column file of that entry can list a field that the struct contains" next to the rule in the `column_files` field section ("A field ID may appear in `field_ids` of at most one column file")? Then the overlap rules are in one place.

I'd like to take ownership of investigating and preparing a fix for this issue, if no one is already actively working on it.

The reported race condition in `JdbcLockFactory.initializeLockTables()` appears to occur when multiple Flink maintenance operators concurrently check for the lock table's existence and attempt to create it.

My proposed approach is to:

1. Add regression coverage for concurrent lock-table initialization.
2. Handle the table-already-exists race safely by verifying the table's existence after a conflicting creation attempt.
3. Preserve proper exception handling for genuine JDBC connection failures and other SQL errors.
4. Run the relevant Flink maintenance tests before submitting a PR.

I'm planning to work on this shortly and would be happy to submit a focused PR referencing #18797.

@maintainers, please let me know if there is a preferred approach or if someone is already working on a fix. I'd appreciate being assigned to this issue if appropriate, to help avoid duplicate efforts.

Thanks!

Hi @mxm @pvary, could you review this? It documents #18748 and a workaround validated through stop-with-savepoint → spec change → rewrite → rebuild and restore, on main and a non-main branch.

The prototype fix in #18747 writes deletes across historical specs, but requires a serializer-version change. In addition, it only supports partitioning based on equality fields and still misses Dynamic Sink changes within one checkpoint. Given that complexity, limited coverage, and v4’s prohibition on new equality-delete files, I’m leaning toward landing these docs rather than pursuing #18747.

As a follow-up, I’d suggest a startup check that rejects upsert/CDC writers using a partitioned spec when the target branch contains data files under another spec. That would turn existing mismatches into an explicit error instead of silent incorrect results. Runtime spec changes would need separate handling. Does that direction make sense?

Thanks @adiranjan25. A predicate-side helper that leaves the bound ordering alone is the fix I had in mind, so I'll review here instead of sending a second patch.

Two places still compare with the plain comparator, so `x = 0.0` can still miss `-0.0` rows:

Since it's in the same module, I'd fix it in this PR.
2. `ParquetDictionaryRowGroupFilter` in `parquet`. `eq` and `notEq` build the dictionary set with `lit.comparator()` and call `contains`, so a row group whose dictionary only holds `-0.0` gets skipped for `x = 0.0`. This is intentional, following `client-go` behavior: callers never wait for a reload. "Fresh" here only means "read less than one reload interval ago", not "valid". The held token was valid when read, and producers rotate tokens well before they expire (Kubernetes at 80% of the TTL). Returning only fresh tokens would mean making concurrent callers wait for the reload, which puts file I/O on every request's path, for no gain.

I think what might be confusing here is that we traverse the delta snapshots from latest to oldest. In that order we can check whether a file in the same range has been added + removed, which is the only problematic case for the non-ordered reader.

When we only ever add XOR remove a specific data file, there is no problem at all. When we add and then remove it in the same range, we will detect the removal first, emit the removal (which will remove nothing), and once we get to the add, we check whether we have already removed the data file and skip it entirely. That way we can emit the read requests with a single traversal of the snapshot chain.

body: I think the FieldStats test would best be in the adapter integration PR as that is the boundary which actually writes these bounds into FieldStats. I went ahead and duplicated both. My rationale for duplicate is that the adapter would only read the bounds, so we don't need a full copy, but duplicate costs almost nothing and means one bound can't be affected by reading the other. For example, with identity both bounds would be the same buffer, so if the adapter wrote the lower bound with a relative read, the upper bound would then be empty and get written as a too-small bound, causing files to be incorrectly pruned.

body: Updated so null partition values and non-order-preserving transforms both return null instead of throwing. For context, I originally wrote this utility with the intent that callers (specifically the adapter) would always check if the value is null and only call it for monotonic transforms, but that's really a choice about how we implement the adapter, and handling it here is clearer. I think returning null is better than returning `<null, null>` because when the partition value is null every source value is null, so there are no bounds at all. A null upper already means unbounded in PartitionSourceBounds, so `<null, null>` would mean "non-null values exist, but we don't know their range", which isn't true for an all-null partition. Callers would still have to special-case it to avoid reporting bounds for a column with no non-null values, so returning null makes that case explicit.

With `distZip` as the only unclassified artifact, Gradle derives the POM packaging from it, so the published POM should end with `<packaging>zip</packaging>` and no `-sources.jar` / `-javadoc.jar` alongside.
Central requires sources and javadoc jars for any packaging other than `pom`, and the close of the staging repository on repository.apache.org can reject it for that, which would block the RC.

Can you check the output of `generatePomFileForApachePublication` for this module?

Two ways to fix it:
- add `artifact sourceJar` and `artifact javadocJar` (both tasks are already created for this project above), or
- set `pom.packaging = 'pom'` and publish the zip with a classifier.

If the `hive` distribution is added here as @kevinjqliu suggested, a classified `hive` zip doesn't change this: the main zip remains the unclassified artifact.

Sorry for raising this so late. After some offline discussions, I’m wondering whether we should enforce `all entries for a given key must be in the same file` in the index spec, as this may be difficult to maintain for certain (admittedly more extreme) use cases. For a very common key that keeps receiving new entries, each new entry would require rewriting the region file to add another line, and at this point we will need to trade between:
- Higher rewrite costs: Each new entry for that key triggers another rewrite of the region file. To satisfy the same-file requirement, the file would keep growing, making each rewrite increasingly expensive.
- Lower index usability: Updating the index less frequently to allow the rewrite to catch up/keep rewrite costs manageable would make the index less likely to be up to date, and therefore less usable for non-time-travel queries.

On the other hand, if we allow entries for a given key to span multiple region files, I think we could avoid this tradeoff by splitting those entries across more files whenever needed.

body:
Thanks, this is a valid concern for hot keys.

The main target is keys that are almost unique, like primary keys, where duplicates are rare. For these, the same-file rule costs nothing, and a lookup reads exactly one region file.

Allowing a key to span multiple region files would change the read path in two ways:
- If the matched `max_ordering_key` equals the key, the reader also has to check the next tracking file entry. This is a small cost.
- A lookup may need to read an unbounded range of region files instead of one. That is a structural change, and may need a scan-like plan instead of a single file read.

Indexes with hot keys can already get this flexibility by ending the ordering key with a unique field, like `[ bucket(256, user_id), user_id, _row_id ]`. Region boundaries can then split a hot key, and lookups prune on the ordering key prefix. New rows get increasing row IDs, so a refresh rewrites at most the last region file of the key. This way only these indexes pay for multi-file lookups.

I left this as a comment in another thread, but expire snapshots is a different beast from all the other actions. It's about removing history, and to accomplish that the only thing we *really* need to do is erase the snapshots from the metadata.json file. The other part of the action, cleaning up files, is not really critical to success. If we don't clean up some files that we otherwise should have, it's not a huge deal.

So basically we're doing the same thing here we were always doing: if we find some file we're supposed to delete and it's not there, we log a warning and move on.

For every other action, failing to read a manifest means the table is corrupted. If I try to rewrite a table or its manifests and a manifest isn't there, that's a failure, and a "partial success" still leaves us with a corrupt table. Orphan removal is even worse: it uses the manifests of live snapshots to decide what's still referenced, so skipping a missing manifest would make its data files look like orphans and we'd delete them. That turns a repairable table into permanent data loss. This is also why the valid-files side of expire stays strict in this PR.

So I'd keep `SkipMissingManifest` private to […]

body:
Taking a step back, here is my motivation for the refactor: I found that in terms of encryption support, our readers are asymmetric now, e.g. Spark readers can read encrypted data and deletes files, but `GenericReader` and `IcebergInputFormat` can't read encrypted delete files, while `EqualityConvertReader` can't read neither encrypted data nor delete files. The idea is to wire-in `InputFilesDecryptor` into the readers where we get it guaranteed that given a `ScanTask` by the reader we have all the referenced files involved with decryption, eliminating asymmetry.
Other motivation is that whenever we add new set of files, e.g. ColumnFiles into the picture, we don't forget to implement encryption support for them. Doing that in `InputFilesDecryptor` solves this too.

The above proposal makes `referencedFiles` in Spark redundant with what `InputFilesDecryptor` is meant to do.

The goal is to allow more general column replacements by making writers avoid ambiguous situations. Unlike my earlier rules, this requires writers to be more aware of exactly which values they are overwriting, but it allows more generic replacement.

The key rule we are trying to respect is:

"Listing a nested field does not change whether its parent struct is null. To change that, the column file must list the parent struct."

3. An added column file must list:

i think mostly looks good (use minor great-arc between endpoints for the SPHERICAL edge interpolation), but can you explain the rationale for some of the impl decisions?

- Arc-containment checks use a 1e-12 tolerance.
- Cross-product lengths at or below 1e-6 trigger conservative handling: nearly antipodal endpoints produce world bounds; short arcs get latitude padding based on their angular length.
- Computed latitude extrema are widened outward by the larger of 1e-6° or a 1e-7 relative margin, clamped to ±90°.
- Longitude coverage follows the shorter circular interval (the shorter one around the world), representing antimeridian crossings with west > east. Computed bounds reaching a pole expand to all longitudes.

body:
Good catch, min/med/max on a driver-side value just repeat the total, which isn't useful.

I looked at moving it to `currentMetricsValues()`. In Spark 4.1, `WritingSparkTask` collects the task metrics once, right before it calls `DataWriter.commit()`, and our `commit()` is where the writer gets closed and the buffered rows are flushed. So there are basically two options:

1. Keep it on the driver (what the PR does now). The write and close totals are both accurate, but min/med/max show the total.
2. Report `writeDuration` from the tasks through `currentMetricsValues()`. That gives a real min/med/max, but only for the row-level write calls. The close time can't be a task metric, so it still goes through the commit messages with only a total. For files smaller than a row group I think most of the actual I/O happens in that close, so the per-task numbers could understate the slow tasks.

Neither is great. What do you think, would you prefer one of these, or is there another way you'd go about it?

body:
This `finally` covers the failure behind the timeouts. On 2.2 and 2.3, `StreamTask.cleanUp` calls `disableInterruptOnCancel()` and `Thread.interrupted()` before `resourceCloser.close()`, where `closeAllOperators` is registered, so cancellation can't interrupt `awaitTermination` inside `close()`. The double close can only come from `processWatermark` leaving a closed service behind.

Only 2.2 and 2.3 hang, although #18815 backported `testConvertEqualityDeletesWithRewriteEnabledE2e` to 1.20 as well. Since 2.2, `Task.doRun` closes `invokable.cleanUp` inside its failure handler, so an exception from `close()` ends in "FATAL - exception in exception handler of task" and stops the only TaskManager, while 1.20 adds it as a suppressed exception. The 2.2 tree has hit the same timeout on main since Nov 9, so it needs this fix too.

Now reads of those locations become unauthenticated GETs, while `newOutputFile`, `deleteFile`, and listing still send the same location to S3. body:
I'm concerned about the client lifecycle. `BaseFileIO` always goes through `fromLocation` without a client, so every `newStream()`, `getLength()`, and `exists()` builds and tears down its own `CloseableHttpClient` and pool. On a Parquet read that's a new TLS handshake for the footer and for every column stream, with no connection reuse, and `io.http.max-connections`/`connections-per-route` don't do anything. The shared-client path is only used by tests, so the tests don't cover the path production uses. The client lifecycle should track with the FileIO: create it lazily, pass it in, and close it in `close()` like `S3FileIO` does with its S3 clients. Then the null-client branches, `hasSharedClient()`, and the per-stream `closeClient` can go away.

Following some research and implementation feedback from https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18676/changes, I’m leaning toward keeping `vector(E, D)` as an Iceberg primitive.

The implementation in [#18676](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18676) strengthens that preference. `VectorType` fits into the existing primitive-type machinery, with `E` and `D` as type parameters and the existing schema serialization path handling the type. A vector field has its normal field ID, with no additional element field ID. This seems natural for a single schema value, similar to `fixed(L)`.

Other databases provide precedents for both approaches:

- Oracle explicitly classifies VECTOR as a [scalar type family in PL/SQL](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/lnpls/sql-data-types.html).
- [pgvector defines vector as a PostgreSQL base type](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector/blob/master/sql/vector.sql), which PostgreSQL describes as a [base/scalar type](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtype.html#SQL-CREATETYPE-BASETYPE).
- Cassandra includes VECTOR among [native types](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/stable/cassandra/developing/cql/types.html), sep […]

body:
Thanks for the fast response!

I think appending `_row_id` is a useful strategy, though:
- The strategy must be chosen at index creation: Since the ordering key is immutable, an existing index cannot adopt this optimization without creating a replacement index. If unexpected skew later makes splitting necessary to keep maintenance viable, the index would violate the proposed same-file requirement by doing so. My concern is making that adaptation depend on an upfront definition choice which is not that easy to predict.
- The maintenance problem arises well before unbounded read fanout: A lookup spanning an unbounded number of index files is a valid worst-case concern. But a more moderate case is a key receiving enough new entries that repeatedly rewriting its region prevents maintenance from keeping up. Splitting those entries across a few files could make updates manageable while still providing a substantial benefit over scanning the source table. The single-file guarantee therefore imposes a concrete maintenance cost even where multi-file lookups would remain useful.

body:
Another confirmation of this leak. In our case the trigger was an S3 write failure while the task's writers were being closed (`SinkWriter.close()` → "Failed to close partitioned delta writer"); the write failure itself was a permissions issue on our side. The task was killed, but its coordinator thread kept running in the Connect worker JVM with the old catalog, attempting a commit every cycle on its own schedule regardless of task restarts. Only restarting the worker clears it.

#18909 fixes the leak, not the write failure: `CommitterImpl.close()` now stops the coordinator even when stopping the worker throws, and still rethrows the original error. Any failure in `stopWorker()` (network, storage, permissions) no longer leaves a coordinator behind.

Relation to #18039: fencing ends a leaked coordinator once a new coordinator starts and the old one makes its next transactional write. It doesn't prevent the leak, so if the connector stays failed, is paused, or is deleted, the thread and its Kafka clients and catalog keep running until the worker restarts. The two changes are complementary.

body: Thanks @pvary for taking a look and the comment. Sharing is the better direction, and Hive already does it: CachedClientPool is a static cache. For the other catalogs it isn't the case today. A RESTSessionCatalog creates its own HTTPClient with a connection pool, auth session, FileIO and a one-thread rest-metrics-reporter pool per instance, and JdbcCatalog creates its own JdbcClientPool. All of these are released only by close(), which is why BaseMetastoreCatalog, RESTCatalog and InMemoryCatalog are Closeable. The static Flink sink already closes its catalog (TableLoader), and so does Kafka Connect (IcebergSinkTask). The dynamic sink operators are the exception: each loads a catalog from the CatalogLoader and never closes it. This only aligns them, and it wouldn't get in the way of pooling later. If you'd rather have the dynamic sink share one catalog per JVM, I'm happy to look at that instead. Which do you prefer?

body:
Previously this was deterministic: expiry was unknown for opaque tokens, so the retry always repeated the normal exchange (hence `times(2)`).

Now the outcome depends on whether the retry (100ms + 0–9ms jitter) lands after the 1s expiry, and the margin is only a few ms, since the refresh is scheduled ~100ms before expiry.

It seems that, if the retry lands early, a second exchange with the old token could happen, and `verify(adapter)` could fail. Could we use a larger `expires_in`, or assert only that the credential-based exchange eventually happens?

Thanks! The first target is a key index, where keys are unique except for rare mistaken duplicates, so skew does not occur. The workaround is only needed when the index type is used outside its intended scope.

We discussed the maintenance case at length on the syncs, and chose the single-file rule because index read performance is paramount, and relaxed rules tend to get used beyond their intent. Also, adding a key's new entries without rewriting its region file only works for inserts. Deletes would again need either rewrites or delete files in the index, which adds significant complexity.

We agreed to revisit this once we have more data points, so the decision is not final. A new index format version could allow splitting keys.

body:
Not per sign request, but per `FileIO` instance. And we could have hundreds if not thousands of those in the same JVM.

A freshly-created Caffeine cache cost little memory, but if the cache is per `FileIO`, this means that 2 `FileIO`s belonging to the same principal cannot share the cache, which results in more calls to the sign endpoint than necessary.

Instead, I would keep the cache static, but would change the cache key.

But adding `token` or `client:secret` only to the cache key is not enough. Other auth managers may include other types of credentials, and since 1.12, catalog servers can also send credential-like data in the `remote-signing-config` object: these should be part of the cache key as well. As an extra protection, I think that the endpoint URI should also be part of the cache key.

In conclusion, the cache key should include the whole `properties()` map. Two clients with identical properties are indistinguishable to any signing server, and can safely keep sharing cache entries. The signing endpoint, the credentials and the remote signing configuration are all derived from them, and are thus included automatically.

Including the whole properties map doesn't hurt t […]

Hi maintainers,

I've submitted this PR as initial regression coverage for the subset-key `MERGE INTO` partition-grouping behavior discussed in #18597.

The tests reproduce the difference in partition grouping with partially clustered distribution enabled versus disabled, while verifying MERGE correctness.

I'd appreciate technical feedback on three points:

1. **Regression coverage:** Does this test adequately capture the partition-concentration behavior described in #18597? Are there additional scenarios or assertions that would make the coverage more valuable?
2. **Technical significance:** How important is this behavior for Iceberg users running large-scale MERGE workloads, and what additional evidence would help establish its practical impact?
3. **Next implementation:** Would an Iceberg-side planning improvement or node-local shuffle mechanism be the appropriate next step, or is there a preferred alternative?

I'm happy to strengthen the tests, run additional reproducible benchmarks, and contribute a follow-on implementation based on maintainer guidance.

Thank you for reviewing this contribution.

body:
Thanks for the review! This is still decided by field id. The loop goes through each field id in the old schema and looks up the same id in the new schema. Since field ids never change, an id is missing from the new schema only when that field, or a parent of that field, was dropped. So the result is deterministic, and the only new entries are the fields nested under a dropped or renamed column.

Agreed that these properties are only meaningful for leaf columns. That is why this change is needed. For example, with `location struct<lat, long>` and a property on `location.lat`, `deleteColumn("location")` used to only look at `location` itself, so the property on the leaf `location.lat` was left behind. The new code includes the leaf columns, so it is removed. List element and map key/value paths work the same way, e.g. a property on `points.element.x` is removed when `points` is dropped.

Non-leaf names like `location` or `points.element` are also in the list, but they don't match any property, so they have no effect.

Users can drop columns that are still referenced by historical partition specs. After the drop, those specs resolve the source column's type as `unknown`, so for files written under them we can't fill the source column bounds from the partition value. For identity and truncate the partition value's type is `unknown` too. For year, month, day and hour the partition type is fixed, but the source could be a date or any of the timestamp types, and their bounds are encoded in different units.
Ideally we'd get the source column's type from an older schema, but expire snapshots can technically remove every schema that has it while files under that spec are still live. Arguably that's an issue in expire snapshots, because it keeps a spec while removing the schemas that spec still references fields for.

Right now i just fail this case to prevent producing metadata that would lead to an inability to reconstruct the tuple but I think we'll need to address this.

body:
Thanks for the detailed write-up @Simanchal-Liveramp! The use case makes sense, but how to achieve it depends on where you want the token exchange to happen.

Two setups can be considered:

1. The exchange happens outside Iceberg: use `rest.auth.type=bearer`. A producer (e.g. a sidecar) performs the RFC 8693 exchange and writes the access token to a file, which Iceberg re-reads periodically. The producer owns the refresh schedule and writes a new token ahead of expiry, which is the whole point of this design. If the catalog validates the projected service account token directly, that file can even be used as is, without any exchange. Otherwise, you could write a small sidecar that reads the projected service account token file, does the exchange, and writes the resulting token to another file.
2. The exchange happens inside Iceberg: ideally, use `rest.auth.type=oauth2`. Fetching a token, refreshing it based on its expiry and retrying are exactly what an OAuth2 client does. The bearer manager deliberately never contacts an authorization server or performs an OAuth2 grant. Unfortunately, this is not possible today, but sounds like a good enhancement for the new OAuth2 manager v2 (#18 […]

body:
Thanks for looking into the options. Before choosing one, I'd like to step back on the motivation.

Spark already shows per-task duration (min/med/max). For example, with 3 tasks:

| Task | Sort (not Iceberg) | Iceberg write() | Iceberg close() | Task duration |
|------|--------------------|-----------------|-----------------|---------------|
| 1    | 5 s                | 2 s             | 3 s             | 10 s          |
| 2    | 5 s                | 2 s             | 3 s             | 10 s          |
| 3    | 5 s                | 16 s            | 9 s             | 30 s          |

Today Spark shows 10 s / 10 s / 30 s, so we can see task 3 is slow, but not whether Iceberg is the cause.

With this PR, we get writeDuration = 20 s and writeCloseDuration = 15 s for the whole job. That doesn't tell us which task the time came from, so we still can't tell that task 3 is slow because of the Iceberg write.

Option 2 would show 2 s / 2 s / 16 s for write(), but close() would still be a total, and as you mentioned, for small files most of the time is in close().

What would a user do with these these metrics that they can't do today?

Also, write() is called once per row, so this adds two […]

Thanks for the check, it also get me thinking maybe instead o relying on the internal state such as deleted or renamed, maybe we can iterate the existing table properties instead. This help ensure the new schema indexing is only triggered when there's existing column level configurable table properties set on the table.

So the basic idea is to find all existing properties with column properties prefix, to get the existing field names, then use old schema to find the field id and then look up the field id in the new schema to see if rename or drop happens.
- if leaf field or parent struct renamed, then the new property key will be `prefix + newName`
- if leaf field or parent struct dropped, then can skip this line in new properties

the main use case for us is the stage-level breakdown, not per-task attribution. for a write stage we want to know how much of the time goes to shuffle/sort vs actually writing to object storage (ABFS in our case), so we know what to tune: shuffle partitions and sort on one side, file sizes, write parallelism and storage settings on the other. today the stage only shows task duration, which mixes all of that together. with the totals, in your example we can see 35 s of the 50 s task time is the Iceberg write + close, so it's the storage write that needs tuning, not the sort.

body:
Thanks for pushing on this, you were right to ask. WritersBenchmark actually doesn't go through SparkWrite's DataWriter (it calls ClusteredDataWriter/FanoutDataWriter directly), so I wrote a small local JMH that drives SparkWrite's own writers with the same 2.5M-row Parquet setup, and compared the PR against the PR minus the per-row timer.

The overhead is visible on the unpartitioned path. It was 4% to 12% slower across four separate runs, about 60 to 190 ns per row, and the no-timer variant matched main. On the partitioned paths the difference was within noise on my (pretty busy) box. The lambda mostly gets scalar-replaced, but in the fanout writer some JVM forks did allocate it per row (+16 to 40 B/row). And it's the nanoTime calls themselves rather than the lambda: an inline nanoTime version without the lambda was even slower. A nanoTime pair is ~49 ns here.

So I'll take per-row timing out of write(). I'm thinking of timing at the output stream instead (wrap the FileIO we give OutputFileFactory), so we only read the clock per buffer flush, and keeping the close timing. That still separates storage time from shuffle/sort, which is what I was after. Does that sound reasonable?

On clientBuilder/clientPoolBuilder, I checked how they behave today. The Flink CatalogLoaders go through CatalogUtil.loadCatalog (no-arg constructor, then initialize), so the builders are never set and each catalog owns its client or pool. A catalog also closes whatever its builder returns. JdbcCatalog.close() closed an injected shared pool, and a second catalog on that pool then failed with "Cannot get a client from a closed pool". RESTSessionCatalog.initialize calls the builder twice and closes the first result immediately. Sharing through those hooks would need the builder to return something whose close() is safe, or a contract change in the catalogs.

The rule already used in the repo is that whoever loads a catalog closes it: TableLoader.CatalogTableLoader.close() (called from IcebergFilesCommitter.close()) and Kafka Connect's IcebergSinkTask. This PR applies that to the dynamic sink operators. I'm happy to follow whatever policy you, @nastra , @mxm and @Guosmilesmile settle on. If the decision is not to close catalogs, I'll close this PR.

I took out the per-row timing from `write()` everywhere and kept the close timing.

Instead, `TimedFileIO` goes into `OutputFileFactory` through `ioSupplier` and times the storage calls (create, write, flush, close) on each output stream, so the clock is read per stream call, not per row. | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `WHERE d >= 0.0` | `[2]` | | `[1, 2]` |
| `WHERE d IN (0.0, 7.0)` | `[]` | | `[1]` |
| `WHERE d < 0.0` | | `[1]` | `[]` |

Since #13234, `rest.client.user-agent` has been a full override of the header. With this PR, the same value is now treated as "caller tokens" and `iceberg-java/<version> (jvm …)` is appended.

That is the most straightforward approach, but is also a silent behavior change for existing users. For example, `rest.client.user-agent=MyApp/1.0` used to send exactly `MyApp/1.0` and would now send `MyApp/1.0 iceberg-java/1.11.0 (jvm 17.0.9)`.

Most people won't mind, but anyone matching on the exact header (proxy rules, server-side filters, dashboards) would be affected.

Would it be worth considering a separate property for the new behavior, for example `rest.client.user-agent.prefix`, and leaving `rest.client.user-agent` as a full override? That way:

- existing configs keep working unchanged;
- the new property's purpose is obvious from its name;
- an escape hatch remains for deployments that need to control the whole header.

This turns the filter's field IDs into names using the current schema. I see two problems:

1. If the filter uses a field ID that is only in an older schema, loadTable fails. But column projections are checked against all schemas (RESTTable line 58), so the two parts follow different rules.
2. For time travel, DataTableScan binds against the snapshot's schema (useSnapshotSchema() is true), so the name-based filter binds by name there. If the column was renamed, the read fails. If names were swapped (a -> b, b -> a), the filter binds to the wrong column and returns rows it should hide.

The spec asks for field-ID references so the filter survives renames. Could we keep the filter bound by ID instead of converting to names here?

| 7 in table1 + 3 in table2 | the table1 client gets 5 keys; the **table2 client** gets table1/f5, table1/f6 and the 3 table2 keys | each client gets only its own table's keys |

So there's a second case besides the remainder going to the root client. On `main`, batches are grouped only by bucket, so one batch can hold keys from several prefixes. It is then sent with the client of whichever path filled it. So any `deleteFiles` call whose paths span more than one credential prefix can send some keys with another prefix's credentials. Grouping by client as well, as this PR does, fixes both cases.

body:
Potential repeated index construction across manifests?

Since lazyMetricsEvaluator is scoped to each ManifestReader, every reader constructs its own InclusiveMetricsEvaluator, which in turn calls PartitionedInLiterals.build(expr, spec).

For scans involving many manifests with the same partition spec and row filter, this repeatedly binds the same expression and rebuilds the same bucket-to-literals index.

Could we consider reusing the evaluator at the scan-planning level, keyed by partition spec, similar to the evaluator caching already used in ManifestGroup?

This would reduce index construction from once per manifest to once per partition spec per scan, without changing file-pruning behavior.

The impact may be negligible for smaller scans, but it would be worth benchmarking with a large number of manifests and a 200–400+ value IN predicate.

body:
Short-circuit empty candidate sets before checking bounds.

`PartitionedInLiterals.literalsFor()` can return an empty collection when no `IN` literals map to the file's partition value.

Currently, `in()` continues to evaluate the lower bound and returns `ROWS_MIGHT_MATCH` if it is missing or NaN, even though an empty candidate set already proves the predicate cannot match.

Could we add an early return here?

```java
if (literals.isEmpty()) {
  return ROWS_CANNOT_MATCH;
}
```

This would allow the partition-aware metrics evaluator to reject such files independently of column statistics.

I recognize that `ManifestReader` normally applies partition pruning first, so the practical impact may be limited. Still, this seems like a small, correctness-preserving improvement. It may also be worth extending the null-bucket test to cover missing bounds.

body:
For bucketed IN predicates, transform.project() is more expensive than a capability check. Bucket.project() calls ProjectionUtil.transformSet(), which applies the bucket transform to every literal and constructs an intermediate projected predicate.

Since we're only checking whether the result is non-null, that projected predicate is discarded. We then bind the same transform and apply it to every literal again when building literalsByValue.

This effectively hashes the same IN literals twice per index construction, along with the additional intermediate allocations.

Could we avoid the full projection here through a lightweight eligibility check, or otherwise reuse the transformed values?

This also compounds the per-manifest index reconstruction cost discussed earlier. It would be interesting to benchmark the impact with larger IN lists, especially for string keys.

Not a correctness concern, but potentially an easy opportunity to reduce planning overhead.

The tracking wrapper is split into leaf and root `getInternal` implementations because the two write schemas no longer share a prefix: leaf tracking omits `deleted_positions` and `replaced_positions`, so the appended `snapshot_timestamp` is at position 6 in leaf manifests and 8 in root manifests.

body:
Thanks, good catch on where the index lives. A couple of data points:

- The per-reader binding predates this change: ManifestReader already builds its own Evaluator and InclusiveMetricsEvaluator lazily for each manifest. What this PR adds per reader is the literal index, one bucket hash and map insert per IN literal, built only for manifests that survive manifest-level pruning. With the project() call removed (see the PartitionedInLiterals thread), each literal is now hashed once.
- The JMH run in the description opens a new ManifestReader per op, so it rebuilds the index every iteration. In the 400-literal case where nothing can be pruned (pure overhead), allocation rose from 13.34 to 13.76 MB/op and time was within noise (18.04 ± 9.27 vs 18.12 ± 8.32 ms/op), compared with decoding the 10,000-entry manifest.

Caching evaluators per spec in ManifestGroup would also remove the existing per-reader binding, but it means passing a prebuilt evaluator into ManifestReader (and DeleteFileIndex).

I think we can target it as a followup PR and as it's own optimization.
title: Review comment on apache/iceberg#18933 (core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/ManifestReader.java)

body:
Good point. The project() call was only there to exclude transforms that can't narrow (void returns null, and unknown transforms can't be bound). I replaced it with a PartitionSpecVisitor(IsBucketTransform) that accepts only bucket fields, so the literals are hashed once, when building the index, and no projected predicate is built. Behavior is the same for every built-in transform.

On the benchmark, the change didn't move allocation measurably on the 400-literal integer case (13.76 vs 13.74 MB/op), so most of the per-reader cost is the index maps themselves. String keys hash more expensively, so the saving there should be larger, but I haven't measured it.

On breaking when we see a file: I'd keep it working. `PositionDeletesTable` goes through this path for every table, so throwing on a file would make position_deletes unusable for any table that has a file column.

There's still one gap in the current version, though. The position_deletes `GetID` matches by ID value, so any `row.*` column whose ID equals a partition field ID (both start at 1000) gets reassigned too. A plain column just gets silently re-IDed, but a file column now throws. I reproduced it on 9ed30e4 with a wide table whose file column lands on ID 1000, partitioned by `identity(id)` (partition field 1000):

```
new PositionDeletesTable(table)
-> UnsupportedOperationException: Cannot reassign file field 1000 to 1007: this GetID does not implement get(int, Type)
```

The same table with a string column at 1000 loads fine. Partition fields are never file-typed, so could the `GetID` in `PositionDeletesTable.calculateSchema` override `get(int, Type)` and return `oldId` for file types? I'm happy to share the test if it helps.

body:
One concern about the compatibility claim. @InvisibleProgrammer asked about bumping `format-version` in https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/11041#issuecomment-3709796824, and @stevenzwu replied in https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/11041#issuecomment-3873040325 that it isn't needed since there are no breaking changes. That's true for readers, but there's a problem on the writer side.

An MV-unaware writer (e.g. an older Iceberg Java client running `ALTER VIEW ... SET TBLPROPERTIES` against a non-REST catalog) would silently remove `storage-table`, since it drops unknown fields when rewriting the metadata. The MV would become a plain view and the storage table would be orphaned. I don't think we can prevent this with spec text, because old libraries can't tell an MV from a view.

What do you think about revisiting the bump? Old engines would then fail on MVs instead of silently dropping them.

body:
Thanks for the detailed analysis!

I cited the expressions spec for the comparison rules of the other primitive types (boolean, string, binary, fixed, uuid, decimal, int, long, dates, timestamps), since those are only defined there.

For float/double I cited the table spec sort order. The expressions spec defines NaN equality but not a sort order: `-NaN`, `5.0`, `NaN` can be arranged in any order under its rules, and the index needs a total order. **I'd rather not introduce a third float ordering.**

Lookups are for single values, and each key maps to one region file. When predicate semantics require matching both `-0.0` and `0.0`, or both `-NaN` and `NaN`, the reader does two point lookups, reading at most two region files.

You're right that the base rule and the float bullet disagreed. I split the rules, so float/double use the table spec sort order and the other types use the expressions spec comparisons.

You're also right that the table spec's "aligns with Java" claim is inaccurate. Implementations must follow the spec order, not Double.compareTo. It should be fixed in a separate PR.

body:
recording an offline discussion with Andrei:

Ideally, we would like `collation` to be a part of the NestedField's attributes, so the collation can be directly seen by looking at he field. We started with that proposal originally, too.

The reason we changed it: It is currently not clear whether collations will be part of the initial v4 release. If they're not, we can't (to the best of our knowledge) just retroactively add a collation property to NestedField. There might already be engines that support v4 tables but don't know about collations. If any such engine rewrites the schema of a table, it might silently drop collations (by not preserving them), without even realizing it. Given the impact on performance and query behavior, the risk of such an accidental drop seems too high.

So we've been looking for another, safer way to say "this column has collation X" - in a way that engines supporting v4 can't accidentally drop. Using a stat-only field is the best approach we found so far, but I think we're both happy to go another route, if there's a better way

> I'd rather not introduce a third float ordering.

Agreed, and the split fixes the conflict. Two lookups work for signed zero. NaN needs one more rule, but not a new order.

IEEE 754 doesn't specify the sign of a NaN result. For `0.0 / 0.0`, x86 SSE returns the negative default NaN `0xfff8000000000000` ([Intel SDM](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html), Vol. 1, "QNaN Floating-Point Indefinite"), and AArch64 returns `0x7ff8000000000000`. Under this order, the same row's stats-only key for `a / b` lands at the start of the index from one writer and at the end from another. NaNs with different payloads are also distinct keys, so `IS NaN` is two range scans that can span several region files, not two point lookups.

Could the order treat every NaN as one value that sorts after `Infinity`? That is the order #2891 proposed, and Java's `Double.compare` [already implements it](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/2bd60a093a889a44a9e67033dba3abf4c36895f5/api/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/types/Comparators.java#L40-L41), so it isn't a third order. Thanks, the `refs` precedent is a fair point, though I'd see it as a risk we accepted rather than a pattern to follow, and today far more engines and library versions read and write views.

Silently turning an MV into a view isn't really graceful for MV-aware engines. `SHOW CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`, `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` and `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW` would start failing, and users would have to fall back to `DROP VIEW`, which leaves the storage table orphaned. These failures would show up on upgraded engines, far from the old writer that caused them, while a format bump only makes old engines fail, with a clear error.

I like the writer requirement as an addition, since it helps future implementations. I just wonder if it's enough on its own, given that already-released writers wouldn't be covered. Happy to go with whatever the group thinks is best, though.

body: Agreed, that is the rule now. DynamicRecordException is only thrown by in-memory steps that depend on the record's schema, spec, equality and distribution fields or data: the schema comparison, schema and spec evolution (validated with apply() before commit()), and the upsert and distribution checks. Catalog and commit calls are never classified, since their failures can't be told apart from transient ones: the REST client maps HTTP 400 to IllegalArgumentException/ValidationException, Glue throws IllegalStateException, and a closed client pool throws IllegalStateException. To keep the list complete, TestTypeMismatchFailures runs every ordered pair of 25 types, as a column and nested in a struct, list or map, and asserts the outcome is either success or DynamicRecordException. TestTableUpdater#commitFailureIsNotRecordException pins the other side. Two cases that fit the rule only fail inside commit() or table creation: [dropping a partition source column, now covered / not covered], and creating a table with a v3-only type, which depends on the format version the TableCreator picks.

- To determine the relative of the file content and whether delete files apply to a data file
- To set the inherited sequence number of a data file or to set inherited row-level sequence numbers (`_last_updated_sequence_number`)

Thanks! All four follow one rule: bounds can be a bit too big, but should never be too small, because a box that is too small can skip a file with matching rows. So whenever rounding makes a case unclear, the code picks the bigger box. The constants aren't proven minimums. They are much larger than double rounding error (around 1e-16) and much smaller than anything a query cares about (1e-6° is about 0.1 m). I added a short comment for each in [91518cf](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18879/commits/91518cf6878996455ba0046761c3162d028ed25d).

1. `1e-12` arc tolerance: near an endpoint, rounding can flip the sign test and reject a vertex that is on the arc. Accepting one just outside only widens the box by under a meter.
2. `1e-6` cross-product cutoff: the length is `sin(theta)`, so a small value means the endpoints are almost the same or almost opposite, and the normalized plane is unreliable. A short arc can't change latitude by more than its length (about 6 m at the cutoff), so we pad by that. A nearly antipodal edge can flip to the other side of the globe, so only world bounds are safe.

body:
This is currently over-specified and too specific.

It would be better to state that the file's metadata must be updated to reflect the data changes. For example, if the file is no longer sorted according to the order identified by `sort_order_id`, then the sort order must be updated.

We want to avoid statements like "if X then you must Y" because those are rigid and must be completely correct. It's overly rigid because these changes don't necessarily have the required effect. If you replace a sort field but the rows are still in sorted order, this still requires implementations to set the order ID to null (**which, by the way, is not a valid sort order ID**).

A better way is to state consistency requirements, or (better yet) let other parts of the spec state their consistency requirements. Sort order is a good example again: when the sort order ID is set, the file's data must be in that sort order. Then all you need to say here is that the metadata must be consistent. You can't change the data and not worry about the rest of the metadata.

...

@manuzhang Thanks, you're right, `requiresRewrite` had the same issue. When a transaction rewrites a staged manifest with `clusterBy` and then retries, `requiresRewrite` matched the manifests rewritten in the first attempt by path, so the rewrite wasn't redone. The manifests written then were committed with the data sequence number (v2) and first row IDs (v3 and v4) of the first attempt. The new test `rewriteStagedManifestAfterTransactionRetry` shows it: without the change, FILE_A ends up with the concurrent commit's data sequence number, 1 instead of 2, for format versions 2, 3 and 4.

`requiresRewrite` now also compares the inherited metadata (sequence number, min sequence number, first row ID) of each rewritten manifest with the current manifest at the same path, and performs a full rewrite if any of them changed. Unlike a directly deleted manifest, it can simply read the manifest again, so it rewrites rather than fails. Both checks share `inheritsSameMetadata` and a by-path map of the current manifests. Please take another look when you get a chance.

body:
Two details worth noting when designing the fix in `api`:

1. **`Transform.project` / `projectStrict` return type:** Both methods in `org.apache.iceberg.transforms.Transform` (lines 115, 128) return `UnboundPredicate<T>` rather than `Expression`. Representing `x_trunc <= -1000 OR x_trunc == 2147483296` (or `x_trunc > 0 AND x_trunc != 2147483296` for strict projection) requires a compound `Expression`. Without either returning `null` (which disables `<`/`<=` partition pruning for any non-power-of-2 width) or introducing an `Expression`-returning projection hook used by `Projections` and `ResidualEvaluator`, a single `UnboundPredicate` cannot include the wrapped partition without widening the range.

2. **Strict projection for `GT` / `GT_EQ`:** For non-power-of-2 widths, `TruncateUtil.truncateInt` wraps values near `Integer.MIN_VALUE` into the top of the positive range (e.g., `truncate[1000](Integer.MIN_VALUE) == 2147483296`, and for `truncate[7]`, `truncateInt(7, Integer.MIN_VALUE) == 2147483643 < truncateInt(7, Integer.MAX_VALUE) == 2147483646`). body:
For the range case, one `UnboundPredicate` cannot carry the wrapped partition, so the projection has to become compound. I would add an `Expression`-returning default method on `Transform` that delegates to the existing `project` / `projectStrict`, and have `Projections` and `ResidualEvaluator` use it. Truncate can then return `x_trunc <= -1000 OR x_trunc == 2147483296` for `LT` / `LT_EQ`.

For strict `GT` / `GT_EQ`, I would return no strict projection when the wrapped partition is reachable, rather than `AND x_trunc != 2147483296`. That is what apache/iceberg-python#4407 already does, and it leaves the residual evaluator on the original predicate.

I can take this once the approach is agreed. Could a committer assign it to me?

body:
FYI, the token exchange grant in `OAuth2Manager` v1 was never meant to exchange a token with proper RFC-8693 semantics.

The usage described here is one of the unconventional, non-standard ways of triggering a token exchange grant today. It is non-standard on both sides: Trino crafts a JWT instead of passing a valid user token; and Iceberg exchanges it using unrelated client credentials, resulting in a token exchange request that no IDP today would ever accept.

IMHO, this whole workflow should now be considered legacy and deprecated for removal. We need to build this functionality again, from  scratch:

- On the Trino side: provide the real user token, or better yet, provide a fully-fledged `AuthManager`.
  -  See https://github.com/trinodb/trino/issues/26320
  - See https://github.com/trinodb/trino/pull/29758
- On the Iceberg side: land `OAuth2Manager` v2, then implement a proper token exchange grant. In parallel, land `AuthManager` programmatic injection.
  - See https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18756
  - See https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/12655

body:
Do we actually need to define an ordering for vectors? `identity` excludes `vector` and no other transform accepts it. Sort orders can't reference vector fields, and vectors are excluded from `lower_bound`/`upper_bound`. Nothing in Sorting can use this ordering. It also sets up a cycle: expressions-spec.md:169 points here for ordering, and this sentence points back to expressions-spec `#comparisons`. The only thing it enables is `<`/`>` on vectors, and lexicographic order over embeddings isn't meaningful. It's easy to add ordering later if a use case comes up, but hard to take it out once it's in the spec.

I'd drop this sentence and keep vectors equality-only for now. If we do need ordering, it should be defined once, next to the type in the Vector section, not here.

body:
I believe we need one more level of validation for `float16`. Its value type is `float`, and that type drives JSON single-value serialization and the Avro mapping (line 1904 writes 4-byte floats). So what happens with `[0.1, 70000.0]` in a `vector(float16, 2)`? 0.1 isn't exactly representable in binary16, and 70000 overflows to Infinity. Parquet requires exact preservation and can't hold either. "Readers and writers must enforce the vector dimension and element requirements" doesn't cover this, because the element requirements only rule out null, NaN, and infinity. Some readers will round and others will fail, so the same table can return different values depending on the file format.

Something like: "`float16` element values must be finite IEEE 754 binary16 values. When stored or serialized using the `float` value type, the value must be exactly representable as binary16; writers must not produce other values and readers must reject them." Or drop `float16` from this PR. New element types can be added to the table later without breaking anything.

Thanks for writing this down.

After talking with Ryan and Daniel, I moved the collation back into the schema as a field attribute. That is where readers expect to find it.

Your concern still applies. The schema attribute is safe only if v4 includes it from the start. A v4 engine that does not know the attribute can drop it when it rewrites the schema. So the attribute needs to make the v4 cutoff.

It is small: the attribute, its list and map forms, and the name grammar. The bounds can come later, because readers ignore stats-only field types they do not support.

If the attribute misses the cutoff, I will propose the stats-only declaration we discussed as the fallback.

body:
Some languages, such as Java, internally use UTF-16 to represent strings. Java's String does not compare by code points, but by UTF-16 code units. That matters because UTF-16 uses 2 UTF-16 code units (surrogates) to represent code points above U+FFFF.  As a consequence, U+10000 < U+FFFF in Java - which contradicts, e.g., UTF-8 ordering (and code point ordering, too, imho).

I think `Unicode code point` is the correct term to use here. It should be fine to leave it as is, but consider making it explicit to reduce the risk of Java writers providing wrong stats

body:
Hello, I would like to pick this up.

I've reproduced it on `main` with Spark 4.2, and it affects merge-on-read `DELETE` as well as `UPDATE`. `SparkPositionDeltaWrite.BaseDeltaWriter#buildPartitionProjections` projects each spec's `partitionType()` out of `Partitioning.partitionType(table)`. That unified type only keeps partition fields whose source column is still in the schema (`allActiveFieldIds`). Once `p` is dropped, the unified type is `struct<>`, so `StructProjection.create` throws on spec 0's `p` field.

The obvious one-liner, switching to `StructProjection.createAllowMissing`, isn't safe. I tried it: the `UPDATE` commits, but the new position deletes/DVs carry `p=null` while the data files are still `p='a'`, and the next read fails in `DeleteFileIndex.validatePartitionMatch` with "Mismatched partition tuples ... metadata is corrupted". The value can't come through `_partition` either, because once the source is dropped the identity result type becomes `unknown` (`NullType` in Spark).

What I'd propose: on the driver, for scan tasks whose spec has fields missing from the unified partition type, collect each data file's own partition tuple (`task.file().partition()`). Broadc […]
title: Comment on apache/iceberg#19117

body:
Quick update: I tried the writer-side approach above and it still corrupts the table. The delete file gets the right partition value, but because the dropped source column's partition field is now typed `unknown`, the manifest entry stores it as null, so the read fails with the same "Mismatched partition tuples" error. Fixing that properly would need a core change.

So for now I've gone with a safe fallback in Spark 4.2: if a merge-on-read DELETE/UPDATE/MERGE would touch live data files in a spec whose fields are missing from the unified partition type, it runs as copy-on-write for that operation (with a warning), and switches back to merge-on-read once those files are rewritten. Regression tests cover UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE in both modes, format v2 and v3. Happy to switch to failing with a clear error instead if you'd prefer that.

body:
No — namespace property values are still strings only. `dict[str, Any]` was generated by datamodel-code-generator for `type: [object, "null"]` where  it falls back to a generic object and ignores additionalProperties.
The Python file is generated by make generate, not edited manually. I changed this schema to the equivalent OpenAPI 3.1 anyOf form so the generator keeps the value type:
```
         properties:
-          type: [ object, "null" ]
+          anyOf:
+            - type: object
+              additionalProperties:
+                type: string
+            - type: "null"
           description:
             Properties stored on the namespace, if supported by the server.
             If the server does not support namespace properties, it should return null for this field.
             If namespace properties are supported, but none are set, it should return an empty object.
-          additionalProperties:
-            type: string
           examples:
             - { "owner": "Ralph", 'transient_lastDdlTime': '1452120468' }
           default: { }
```
After regeneration, it produces `dict[str, str] | None` instead of `dict[str, Any] | None`.
